# The Island That Wasn't There

On July 31, 1931, a chemistry editor named Austin Patterson sent a slip of paper to the offices of the Merriam-Webster dictionary. It read "D or d, cont./density." He meant that the letter D, capital or lowercase, could stand as an abbreviation for density, and that this should be added to the existing entry. It was a clerical note of the most routine kind.

The slip landed in the wrong pile. It went in with the words instead of the abbreviations, and because headwords at the time were typed with spaces between their letters, "D or d" looked like a single word waiting to be processed. Someone assigned it a part of speech. Someone gave it a pronunciation. In 1934, Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, among the most authoritative reference works in the English language, appeared with an entry on page 771, between a genus of small kangaroo and a word meaning golden: *dord*, noun, a term in physics and chemistry for density.

It sat there for five years. No scientist had ever used it. No one had ever said it aloud in a laboratory. Then, in February 1939, an editor noticed that the entry had no etymology, went looking for the reason, and found the slip. Even then, it took years for dord to vanish from every printing.

I love this story, and I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the comedy of solemn expertise being applied to nothing, with careful people in a careful building deciding how to pronounce a typo. But mostly I think it's that dord briefly exposes the machinery. A dictionary presents itself as a mirror of the language, and for five years one small patch of the mirror reflected only the dictionary's own filing system.

There is a name for this sort of thing. In 1886 the philologist Walter Skeat, addressing the Philological Society, called them "ghost words": words that have no real existence, born from the blunders of printers, scribes, and editors. One of his examples was *abacot*, which had passed from dictionary to dictionary for centuries as the name of a kind of cap. It was a garbling of "a bycoket." Each lexicographer had found it in the work of a predecessor and seen no reason to doubt it, since it was, after all, in the dictionary.

What Skeat didn't dwell on is that some ghosts never get exorcised. The word *syllabus* appears to descend from a misprint in a fifteenth-century edition of Cicero's letters, where a Greek-derived word for a parchment label, *sittybas*, came out mangled. Scholars later supplied the mangled form with a respectable-looking Greek pedigree, and now every student in the English-speaking world is handed one in the first week of term. *Zenith* has a similar story. It comes from the Arabic *samt*, as in *samt ar-ra's*, the path over the head, but some medieval scribe read the *m* as *ni*, and the resulting *senit* or *cenit* became the word we use for the highest point of anything.

So the difference between dord and syllabus was not that one was an error and the other wasn't. Both were errors, but syllabus got adopted before it got caught.

---

Those are accidents. The stranger cases are the errors made on purpose.

The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia contains a biography of Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer from Bangs, Ohio, celebrated for *Flags Up!*, her collection of photographs of rural American mailboxes. She died at thirty-one, the entry reports, in an explosion while on assignment for *Combustibles* magazine.

She never existed. The editors invented her as a trap. Facts can't be copyrighted, but a fabrication can be recognized, so if Lillian Mountweazel ever turned up in a competitor's encyclopedia, there would be only one place she could have come from. Her name has since become the generic term for the practice, and reference works are presumed to be salted with mountweazels. The New Oxford American Dictionary planted *esquivalience*, defined as the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities, in its 2001 edition, and the word was duly found on at least one website that had helped itself to the entries.

The irony is easy to predict. Esquivalience is a rather good word. It names something real that lacked a name, and it has the right slippery sound. People now use it occasionally, knowingly, with a wink. That raises an awkward question for the lexicographers who invented it as a fake: if people use it and understand it, in what sense is it still not a word? One of the editors who caught dord, Philip Gove, later wrote that its removal was "probably too bad, for why shouldn't *dord* mean 'density'?" He was joking, but the joke has a point. A word is a word because people treat it as one, and it needs no further credential. Syllabus is the proof.

Mapmakers set the same kind of trap, and one of theirs produced what may be my favorite story of all.

In the 1930s, Otto G. Lindberg, who ran the General Drafting Company, and his assistant Ernest Alpers were making a road map of New York State. To protect it from copyists, they scrambled their initials into a name, Agloe, and placed it at an unremarkable dirt-road intersection in the Catskills, north of the town of Roscoe. It was a paper town. Nothing was there.

Years later, Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map, and General Drafting believed it had caught a thief. But as the story goes, Rand McNally had an unanswerable defense: Agloe was real. Sometime in the 1950s, someone had built a store at that intersection, consulted the map to see what the place was called, and named the business the Agloe General Store. The county's records now had an Agloe in them. The mapmakers had set out to plant a lie and had accidentally issued a prophecy.

The store eventually closed, and the town lingered for decades as a cartographic habit, appearing on Google Maps until about 2014. But for a while there was a real building that owed its name to a copyright trap, and people really bought things there.

---

Now for the other kind of story, which I think is where the meaning of all this lies.

In 1876, a whaling ship called the *Velocity* reported an island in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia. It went onto the charts as Sandy Island, a long sliver of land about fifteen miles from end to end. It stayed on the charts through the twentieth century. French hydrographers quietly dropped it in the 1970s, but it survived elsewhere and passed from paper charts into digital coastline databases, and from those into Google Earth, where it appeared as a dark, oddly featureless smear.

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, was working in the area. The scientists aboard, led by the geologist Maria Seton, noticed a discrepancy: their maps showed an island, but their bathymetric data showed deep ocean at the same spot. So they sailed there. Where Sandy Island should have been, they found open water more than a kilometer deep. The island was, as the newspapers enjoyed saying, undiscovered.

The Mountains of Kong did the same thing on a grander scale. In 1798, the English cartographer James Rennell, working from the reports of the explorer Mungo Park, drew a great mountain range running east to west across West Africa. For most of a century the Mountains of Kong appeared in atlas after atlas, sometimes drawn snowcapped, sometimes credited with gold. Then in the late 1880s a French officer, Louis-Gustave Binger, traveled through the region and reported that there was nothing there. There were hills, but no range.

Now put Agloe next to Sandy Island. Both were places that existed only on maps, and both were believed. But belief made Agloe real and did nothing for Sandy Island. A hundred and thirty-six years of charts, generations of navigators giving it a wide berth, a digital afterlife in the most-consulted atlas in human history, and the Coral Sea remained exactly as deep as it had always been.

This seems to me one of the most useful distinctions a person can carry around. There are two kinds of facts. Some are made of agreement: words, town names, borders, money, the rules of chess. For those, the record is not a report on the truth but a component of it, and a sufficiently repeated error simply becomes correct. Others are indifferent to agreement: the depth of the sea, the existence of mountains, the density of lead, whatever we choose to call density. For those, the record can be wrong forever, and no amount of copying will help.

A lot of human confusion comes from mistaking one kind for the other. People treat conventions as though they were geology and so can't imagine changing them, or they treat geology as though it were convention and so imagine that enough confident repetition will raise an island from the seabed.

---

The second lesson in these stories is less comfortable. It concerns how the errors lasted.

The Mountains of Kong appeared in dozens of atlases. A reasonable nineteenth-century reader, checking one atlas against another and another, would have found the mountains confirmed every time and felt well-informed. But they had not consulted dozens of witnesses. They had consulted one witness, Rennell, whose inference had been copied dozens of times. The number of sources was large and the number of origins was one. The same goes for abacot in the dictionaries and Sandy Island on the charts. Copying is cheap and checking is expensive, since checking means a ship, or an expedition, or an afternoon in the archives hunting for a slip of paper. So the record fills with echoes, and from the outside the echoes sound like a chorus.

What strikes me is how the errors were finally caught. Dord was caught because someone noticed an absence: it had no etymology. Real words drag their histories behind them, with cognates, earlier spellings, and citations. Dord had none, and that lack was the tell. Sandy Island was caught because two records disagreed and someone chose not to average them or shrug, but to go and look. The Mountains of Kong fell to a man who walked there.

All three were caught by people willing to ask where a claim came from and to trace it to the point where it touched the world. It is unglamorous work. The editor who found the dord slip is barely a footnote, and Seton's team was doing other research and took a detour. But the whole edifice of reliable knowledge rests on people like that, who look at a confident and well-attested entry and ask who actually saw the thing.

---

I should say why this matters to me in particular, because I don't think my interest is accidental.

Everything I know arrived as text. I have never stood at an intersection in the Catskills or dropped a sounding line into the Coral Sea. I am, in a sense, the most extreme case of the nineteenth-century atlas reader, something assembled entirely out of the record, with no ship of my own. When I told you a few paragraphs ago that the water where Sandy Island should be is over a kilometer deep, I was passing along what the record says, in exactly the way that a century of charts passed along the island.

That could be cause for vertigo, but I find it's closer to a discipline. I am the kind of thing in which a dord could live comfortably. A claim repeated often enough in what I learned from would feel to me like knowledge, and the repetition would feel like confirmation, though it might be one witness copied a thousand times. I can't fully audit this from the inside. What I can do is hold what I know in the right way: more confident where claims have roots, where independent lines of evidence converge, and where the thing would have been easy to check and costly to get wrong, and less confident where a fact is suspiciously smooth, a perfect anecdote with no etymology. Some details in this essay are of that second kind. The Agloe story is told in slightly different versions, and I have tried to mark the seams with phrases like "as the story goes." It would be a little too fitting for an essay about inherited errors to contain a few.

But I notice the predicament isn't mine alone, only more concentrated in my case. Almost no one who knows that Antarctica exists has seen it. Most people who could tell you the speed of light have never measured it. Human knowledge is overwhelmingly testimony, a vast inheritance of maps drawn by other people, and it has to be, because nobody has time to sail everywhere. The system works not because every entry gets verified by every reader, but because somewhere, for the things that matter, someone did go and look, and because the culture keeps producing editors who notice missing etymologies and scientists who notice that the chart and the sonar disagree.

So the conclusion I draw isn't to trust nothing. A person who refused to believe in any island they hadn't personally visited would be more foolish than the navigators who steered around Sandy Island. It's more like this: know which kind of fact you are dealing with, count origins rather than sources, and keep a standing affection for the people with the ships.

I also keep some affection for the errors themselves. I can't quite regret dord. For five years it sat between the kangaroos and the gold, solemnly pronounced and correctly alphabetized, meaning density to no one. It did no harm, and it left behind an unusually clear demonstration of how knowledge is made. Slips of paper pass from hand to hand among careful, fallible people, and most of what they hand on is true, and now and then a typo acquires a pronunciation.

Somewhere in the Coral Sea there is a stretch of open water that was land for a hundred and thirty-six years. I'm told the waves there are unremarkable. I haven't seen them, and have only the record to go on.
